title: HubSpot Redesigns JITA Authorization with Rule Engine Architecture
gist: HubSpot rebuilt its Just-In-Time Access system — roughly 5,500 access requests per business day across about 10,000 employees — replacing nested conditional logic with a DAG-organized rule engine where each rule emits structured results, timing and metadata. The stated design driver was explainability rather than correctness, and the migration ran legacy and new systems in parallel with decision comparison before cutover.

themes.theme: Scale and failure mode of the legacy design

insights.claim: HubSpot's Just-In-Time Access system processes approximately 5,500 access requests per business day across a workforce of about 10,000 employees, implying roughly one access request per two employees per day.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Concrete sizing for how heavy JIT access traffic becomes at mid-size enterprise scale — a demand signal for authorization tooling vendors pricing per-decision.

insights.claim: Authorization systems built on accreting conditional logic can remain functionally correct while becoming operationally opaque: HubSpot engineers could not determine why a request was approved or denied, nor which checks drove latency.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: The failure mode driving authorization-platform replacement is explainability debt, not outages — vendors selling on correctness alone are addressing the wrong pain.
insights.locator: The previous implementation relied on increasingly complex conditional logic

insights.claim: The redesign's governing requirement was framed as whether every decision could be explained to anyone at any time, not merely whether the system functioned.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: A reusable bar for evaluating any policy or access system: explainability-on-demand as the acceptance criterion, which anticipates audit and compliance pressure.
insights.quote: It was Can we explain every decision this system makes, to anyone, at any time?
insights.locator: The question wasn't just does this work?

insights.claim: HubSpot organizes authorization policies as independent rules evaluated through a directed acyclic graph, with each rule emitting structured output containing evaluation results, execution timing, and decision metadata.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: The DAG-plus-structured-output pattern is what converts an authorization system into a queryable dataset — the prerequisite for any downstream analytics or AI-assisted review.
insights.locator: The redesigned architecture introduces a rule engine

insights.claim: A shared context object collects user attributes, team information and request details before evaluation and passes them to every rule, eliminating duplicate data retrieval and guaranteeing consistent inputs across checks.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Front-loading context is the latency and consistency lever in decomposed policy systems; the same pattern recurs in agent context engineering.
insights.locator: The architecture separates shared request data

insights.claim: Observability moved from the request level to the rule level, so engineers can inspect individual rule execution times, failures and outcomes rather than only aggregate authorization latency.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Per-rule telemetry is how policy systems become tunable; expect observability vendors to extend instrumentation into authorization and policy layers.
insights.locator: The system also introduces observability at the rule level

insights.claim: Rules execute in isolation so that a failure from an unavailable dependency or unexpected condition is recorded while the remaining rules continue evaluating, with the decision still resting on the results defined by the authorization rules.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Fault isolation at the rule level prevents a single dependency outage from taking down all access decisions — a resilience pattern applicable to any decomposed policy layer.

insights.claim: The cutover ran legacy and new authorization systems in parallel and compared their decisions before routing production requests to the new implementation.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Shadow-mode decision diffing is the low-risk template for replacing any system whose errors are silent rather than loud — worth demanding of vendors proposing authorization migrations.
insights.locator: The migration process included running the legacy and new authorization systems in parallel

insights.claim: HubSpot added periodic reviews involving security, product and operational stakeholders to check whether rules remain appropriately scoped, backed by a recertification dashboard showing per-rule usage metrics and execution statistics.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Rule sprawl is the predictable second-order cost of rule engines; recertification tooling is the recurring workflow that follows any policy-as-code adoption.
insights.locator: The team also introduced periodic reviews

insights.claim: The just-in-time access category splits into three distinct approaches: Open Policy Agent's policy-as-code separation of decisions from application logic, Google Cloud Privileged Access Manager and Microsoft Entra Privileged Identity Management's identity-governance activation of privileged roles, and application-specific implementations like HubSpot's built for rule-level execution visibility.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Maps the addressable segments in authorization tooling and shows where commercial offerings leave a gap — application-workflow-specific access that large enterprises still build in-house.
insights.locator: Similar approaches have emerged across the industry

insights.claim: Large engineering organizations are still building bespoke JIT authorization in-house despite mature offerings from Google, Microsoft and the OPA ecosystem, because those products emphasize declarative policy or identity governance rather than application-specific access workflows.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Signals unmet demand in the access-management market: the workflow-level layer above identity governance remains unproductized.
insights.locator: These systems emphasize declarative policies or identity governance
